common_name: Persian Yellow Rose (Double Yellow Antique Species Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Persian Yellow is a fully double sport of Austrian Briar and, like its parent, was historically important for introducing true yellow into modern rose breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Persian Yellow is a fully double, rich golden-yellow sport of the single-flowered Austrian Briar, offering a fuller, more substantial bloom in the same historically important yellow color that became a key building block for yellow tones in modern rose breeding. It flowers in one intense flush in late spring on a tough, cold-hardy shrub that tolerates poor, dry soil and harsh winters better than most old garden roses. Like its parent species it carries a somewhat pungent scent up close, noted in the species name foetida. It needs only removal of dead or crossing wood after its single spring bloom to stay healthy and well-shaped.

common_name: Harison's Yellow Rose (Historic American Pioneer Yellow Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Harison's Yellow is an extremely cold-hardy, historic American rose that spread west with pioneer settlers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Harison's Yellow tolerates lean, dry soil and severe winter cold better than nearly any other yellow-flowered rose. Bred in New York City around 1830, this tough hybrid became a beloved pioneer-era rose that spread across the American frontier with westward settlers, planted at homesteads throughout the Great Plains and often still found blooming around long-abandoned farm sites. It bears masses of semi-double, bright golden-yellow flowers with a light, sweet fragrance in a single heavy flush in late spring on a dense, suckering, thorny shrub. It is often associated, though not definitively confirmed, with the folk song 'The Yellow Rose of Texas.' Extremely tough and low-maintenance, it needs only removal of dead wood after flowering and tolerates neglect that would kill most modern roses.

common_name: Stanwell Perpetual Rose (Cold-Hardy Repeat-Blooming Scots Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Stanwell Perpetual, dating to 1838, is a rare repeat-blooming hybrid of the Scots rose, unusual for its class.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Stanwell Perpetual tolerates lean, sandy soil and severe cold exceptionally well, reflecting its Scots rose (Rosa spinosissima) parentage. Discovered in England in 1838, it is notable among old garden roses for genuine repeat bloom, producing double, blush-pink flowers that fade to white with a strong, sweet fragrance from late spring through fall rather than in a single flush like most antique roses of similar age. Its fine, ferny foliage and densely thorny, arching canes give it good textural interest even out of bloom. Extremely tough and low-maintenance, it needs only removal of dead or crossing wood to stay healthy and thrives with minimal care in poor, dry sites.

common_name: Frühlingsgold Rose (Large Single Pale Yellow Spring Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Frühlingsgold ('Spring Gold') is a Kordes hybrid grown for one of the earliest and showiest single-flush rose displays of spring.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, allowing ample room for its large, arching, vigorous growth. Bred by Wilhelm Kordes in Germany and introduced in 1937, Frühlingsgold ('Spring Gold') is a large hybrid shrub rose bred from Scots rose parentage, bearing huge, single to semi-double, soft pale-yellow flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance that open extremely early in spring, often before most other roses have begun to bud. It blooms in one spectacular flush covering the entire large shrub, then rests for the remainder of the season, functioning almost like a flowering hedge or specimen shrub rather than a repeat-blooming garden rose. Extremely cold-hardy and tough, it needs only removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering and tolerates a wide range of soils.

common_name: Frühlingsmorgen Rose (Single Pink-Yellow Bicolor Spring Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Frühlingsmorgen ('Spring Morning') is a Kordes hybrid bred from Scots rose parentage, similar to Frühlingsgold but with a distinctive bicolor bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, allowing ample room for its arching, vigorous growth. Bred by Wilhelm Kordes and introduced in Germany in 1942, Frühlingsmorgen ('Spring Morning') bears large single flowers in a striking bicolor of deep pink petal edges shading to pale yellow at the base, with prominent maroon-red stamens providing further contrast, all carrying a light, sweet fragrance. Like its sibling Frühlingsgold, it blooms in one spectacular early-spring flush on a large, cold-hardy shrub bred from Scots rose parentage, then rests for the remainder of the season. It needs only removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering and tolerates a wide range of soils and harsh winter cold.

common_name: Nevada Rose (Large Semi-Double White-Cream Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Nevada is a large, widely acclaimed shrub rose with a spectacular main spring flush and lighter repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, allowing ample room for its large, arching, densely branched growth. Bred by Pedro Dot in Spain and introduced in 1927, Nevada is one of the most widely acclaimed shrub roses ever raised, producing an extraordinary main flush of large, semi-double, creamy white flowers with golden stamens that can nearly bury the entire shrub in bloom, occasionally flushed pink in cool weather, followed by lighter repeat flowering through summer and fall. Its bold scale and prolific bloom make it a dramatic specimen or informal hedge. Prune lightly to shape and remove old or crossing wood in late winter, and expect the heaviest, most spectacular display in the first flush each spring.

common_name: Marguerite Hilling Rose (Pink Sport of Nevada)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Marguerite Hilling is a pink-flowered sport of the famous white shrub rose Nevada, sharing its size and bloom habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, allowing ample room for its large, arching, densely branched growth. Marguerite Hilling, discovered in 1959 as a pink-flowered sport of the celebrated shrub rose Nevada, bears the same enormous flush of large, semi-double blooms — in warm rose-pink rather than white — that can nearly cover the entire shrub in late spring, followed by lighter repeat flowering through summer and fall. It shares Nevada's bold scale and prolific bloom, making it an equally dramatic specimen or informal hedge for gardeners who prefer pink to white. Prune lightly to shape and remove old or crossing wood in late winter, and expect the heaviest, most spectacular display in the first spring flush.
